I despise the fact that there's no option I could find to show the required moveset on the gameplay screen so that you don't have to keep pausing to the character's control list nor to show the button commands via their controller button (A,B,X,Y). title: Ultimate Chicken Horse
text: This is one of the most fun, funny, cute and clever multiplayer party games out there. Highly recommended. Everything about this game works together really well, and offers full customization to game rules as well as three well-rounded game modes (Creative, Free Play, and Party). Party is really the main mode of the game IMO, where you have limited choices to work with and this keeps the rounds quick and contentious. Creative is probably more satisfying to expert players, or novice players who need to learn the game mechanics. Free Play is primarily for level designers, and there is a level sharing feature to the game, and these custom maps are more or less the basis of the single-player game, where you can challenge and hone your skills on the craziest Mario Hell type levels you desire. The game is fairly easy to pick up, but there is some learning curve for new players, as some of the building elements kinda need to be seen in action to fully understand. Also there are some synergies that can be unexpectedly satisfying, such as firing projectiles through teleporters, and devious use of sticky glue and slippery ice. Wonderfully realized and animated, although I have experienced a couple crashes. My kids have a blast just playing hide-and-seek in the main menu, which says something about how fun and cute the playable characters are to control.

There are also problems with the AI, even on moderate when the AI isn't attacking it is blocking, which makes sense until you realize that only leaves attacking while they are attacking as an option, which usually ends with you hitting each other. I guess if you're the type to dedicate your life and entire being to a game this might be for you but to the average player it just seems cheap and unfair. I can't say enough horrible things about the control scheme of this game it's an absolute nightmare. title: Ultra Street Fighter® IV
text: I remember taking the time to tell all of my friends about how cool I thought MUGEN was, any character you wanted, so many choices, blah blah. And them shooting me down hard, Oh man, MUGEN is a fight simulator bro, it will never amount to more than that... Yet as far as AI is concerned, there are clear resemblences to both. At least in the middle of the generation, you could watch characters throw whiffs and gauge how they felt about fighting, and occasionally you'll get stuck with the distance perfect ai that seemed to punish you for trying anything short of isolating their tyranny. This game seems to tickle that point, and whets itself on the same MUGEN imbalances that make you feel like any grappler is God tier and Ryu is insurmountably better than ken, all the while feeling like Street fighter 2 all over again. What do you mean by that? I mean the same ol, oh boy here's ryu, goodbye high score, or I just failed to ground seth so... Yeah. There are CLEAR cuts in ai and it hurts this game in ways only MUGEN fans could ever begin to understand. Nothing breaks the accuracy of a score than having an upset character exist after a solid line of boring crouch turtles who shouldn't even fight like that at all. Easily put, You can set this game on hardest and not notice until you see characters like Honda and Vega finally feel like attacking now, and Ryu actually knows other moves, and he seems like he can't help but combo into everything. If only all champions of each character could get together and build a solid AI that wouldn't seem exclusive to a challenge... I'd be happy, and also inclined to lock myself into training against it. This game is the bitter taste of choice. One ultra or both. You want to use both? good luck depending on it having the killing power like it used to. Though I highly recommend you use it just for that, so you don't depend on it. Looks like you have to be within an inch of your life to use it, or successfully eat attacks with your focus. So depending on how you can use that, your ultra level may seem easier to obtain. WELL THEN WHY IN THE WORLD DO YOU RECOMMEND IT!? For starters, It's the only fighting game I know with character mods that don't have to be nudes or color swaps. So if you can harass someone to change a character for you, or search long enough, you will find something cool. Next, I think capcom knows that their ai is useless for anything but rage, seriously, where else would focus attacks be extremely useful in pinning someone down? someone will tap you twice and you'll be eating moves, in my opinion the AI is only good for one thing, Spanking jumpers into misery for using a tactic any old time gamer has used since Megaman and Castlevania.... Jump lag reset. If akuma still had that CvS2 Air chop super they would probably not hesitate at all to burn you with that move for even being in the air when he's stocked... So them adding in options such as online training is really nobile of them to do. Then... It's rated the best fighting game of all time! What does that mean? ask activision I don't know... Pick it up just because I guess. But another selling point is that it gives you all the arcade edition costumes. so just take off another 15 dollars of what you think it's worth. In my opinion it's a medium jab to everyone who decided to just upgrade, and a warm welcome to the newcomers. Mixed emotions on that, as newcomers are literally getting the game for an upgrade cost if they can appreciate the dlc. Which I do. Besides, You need the dlc If you want character slots to install the mods to. Also, no more crying about how your character got nerfed and you wish they still let you use them, because allegedly you'll be able to roll back and apparently can when it comes to this game. I don't use certain words because I've never actually bothered building a combo with this game, I can make a few hits work, but since there is no real juggle I just keep it simple. It's a completely new experience. Though to be honest almost all of them were, the jump from 2 to 3. The alpha series, etc. I still prefer alpha to this as a street fighter game, however, If they can polish the AI enough to where I can't cross my fingers through a difficulty and only count on seth to be an upset to my score... This game could end up being a real deal online and off, because it seems for now online is the only real thing that counts, as the highest rated reviews toil of people unhappy with the online system. Regardless... 20$ On gamersgate Right now... Cross your fingers for the dlc outfits going on sale like I am, and happy fighting. It's worth owning, And it adds a new standard to fighting games it actually bothers to support in it's own stubborn... Same game tweaked tricks kind of way...

text: Being an old school Street Fighter fan, and I still have and play Super Street Fighter 2 Turbo (SNES), I thought I would give this new Street Fighter a shot. Today I learned that the SNES controller is much better at Street Fighter  games than my Logitech 310. I crouch hitting my left trigger just to watch my fighter looking at the other fighter without doing a sweep or anything. The control on USF4 is horrible (compared to SSF2T on SNES). I play sports games like FIFA and NBA 2k without any trouble but this game seems to not work unless you button smash. v,>,punch does two moves  and never the actual v,>,punch move when you need it. The game also seems to not realize that you missed a flying kick or punch you cant go striaght into a move while still in the air after a miss but I guess logic has no place in this game. Went to my friends house to pick up his arcade control and this game is amazing. You need the arcade style control to play it which is sad because as a young child I use to play with a gamepad and that's the only reason why I got this game. For Street Fighter fans I would say get it on sale. For someone just getting into Street Fighter I would totally tell you to get this game. I will try to get another gamepad to see if it makes the game better but I doubt it. tl;dr game sucks with a gamepad but is awesome with arcade control 8/10

text: A flash game which should stay on flash game sites. I bought this because it has awesome user rating (90%). I played this game when  I bought it and tried to play again this week to prove my feelings. Yeah, It's definitely doesn't cost your time to play it. So, what is the game about? You are a landlord in kinda magic kingdom. You have 4-16 rooms for rent. Monsters come. If they like your apartments (it depends on its quality), you can let them move in. Each monster give you rent money each period of time. Then you can take a quest. They have different names, descriptions and rewards but do the same. They brings some human warriors to you house. When they come you can call some of you monsters to defend the house. They fight. You win. It repeats some ways. Then you get gold reward from the quest. You can spend gold to buy some stuff to your rooms which increase it attractiveness, so stronger monsters could move in. Then you get new quest, new enemies comes, quest is finished. You get new stuff, new monsters come, then new enemies comes. Actually, that's all. Extremely repetitive. The gameplay after 2 hours is the same at the first 5 minutes. Nothing changes. Is it really interesting to play the game with such gameplay? Pros - Funny setting - Cheap game Cons - SImple gameplay which is kinda boring - Repetitve game. After hours of game time you do the same things which you did in 5 first minutes of the game. - No strategy included - It's not a TD game as it decribed I can't recommend this game because it's boring. text: Unholy heights is a tower defense game where you manage an apartment of monsters. Your monsters must defeat the human forces that pass by. To defeat humans you must rent apartments to monsters. title: Unholy Heights
text: Welcome to Unholy Heights, a cutesy 2D tower defense game with a lot of personality and charm. You are the devil that has just purchased a tenement. Just one tenement, there are no scenarios or anything, just this one tenement in the game. As time goes by, creatures will stop by to visit your apartment building, then they'll want to rent a room assuming you have free rooms. If you take them in, they'll take up residence. This diverse array of creatures will then go about life. They'll head to work, sleep, eat, fall in love, have babies. You really have no control over what they do. The real game comes into play when at the end of the day and night cycle when a hero comes to your apartment to rob it and or kill your creatures. So what do you do to defend your building? Click on your doors to knock on them and they'll come out to fight. The only catch is will they might be at work and not in the apartment. Eventually, the creatures will come back from work and be able to fight if not start fighting when they bump into someone. Each enemy has one of three types of attacks: melee, mid range and long range. Your foes will have the same style of attacks. Its a nice system and since each creature lives in a different room, you can wait for the enemies to get to the center of your building, then call the first and last apartment to pinch them where they can't run away. They can also do the same to you of course. If one of your creatures gets weak, simply click them again and they'll run away to their room, to your devil headquarters or away from the building. These daily attacks are more and less a grind. They won't give you much gold. Instead your tenants will give you daily gold in rent. If you want the most gold, you'll take on quests by clicking the sign on your screen. These quests result in larger enemy amounts in usually 3 waves. These 3 waves take place in short amount of times, so make sure your creatures are healthy. Each of these quests has a star / difficulty rating and bonus gold for completing it. Some quests are mandatory in red, and others are optional, but the optional quests seem more like steps to the red quests. If an enemy gets to the top of your building, they steal gold and try to get away with it. If an enemy makes it out alive, you'll fail the quest and can do it again. It is a very forgiving system that keeps you in the game with no real way to lose. You'll always have creatures wanting to move in if you have an empty building. So what do you do with all of this gold? When you're not being attacked, you can click on a room and see the inhabitants of the room, along with everything in the room. The tenants will want specific things like CD Players, fans, playing cards, plants and so on. You'll need to buy them things and by doing so, your creatures will be able to gain defense, attack and so on. You'll also be tasked with keeping your residents happy, which really seems easy enough. Every type of creature has different needs to become happy. Such as skeletons need to defeat enemies, one type needs to live amongst plants or it'll get sick and other creatures become happy or sad based on the overall joy of the tenement. Some of your creatures will become sad if there are creatures they hate living in the building. The bestiary shows everything. You can raise or lower the rent, and creatures each have jobs, so if they can't meet the rent, they can fall behind. Then it is your choice, do you evict them? Lower their rent? Or just make rent free to keep the good creatures you've worked into deadly killers. When new creatures arrive you can see their job so you know if they're some deadbeat cigarette butt collector or just unemployed in general. That doesn't stop paying tenants from falling in love with unemployed creatures that do nothing. Eventually, you'll be able to add more floors to your tenement, along with unlocking more types of creatures and objects for their homes. Not just that, but you'll see the creatures fall in love and later have babies. What does this all mean for you? When there are 2 creatures living together, that's just more attackers for you. Their babies will grow into adults and be able to fight as well. Creatures can only fall in love and breed with creatures of the same species. There are consumable items such as balloons that will help a resident find love, and erotic cakes that will help a couple make a baby. Of course there are less funny consumable items like health potions as well. Your creatures will gain health when they eat, so you don't really need to micromanage anything. In all, this is a really quirky, one of a kind game that I can highly recommend. The only down side is there seems to be a lot of grinding before you can get through the quests. The game does a great job of explaining things especially compared to other sim games. The game also seems underpriced, but if they had different scenarios, I could understand them having a higher price. The game has the right amount of depth to keep me interested, without overwhelming me.

title: Urban Empire
text: After some discussions in the community forums, I've copied my review/comment - I might change this once a few bugs are fixed. Just as a mid-game review and some context: I got the game for free as a gift. I casually mentioned seeing this game from a sponsored youtube pre-release let's play copy to a friend, and they bought it for me. I feel bad, because I wouldn't have paid for this myself. Currently would not recommend and here are my reasons - encountered at least one graphical bug, I have a GTX1080 on a new rig, running everything Ultra at 4K 60fps fine, but then there are these weird glitches: - silly game breaking save bug: most people play games with a tutorial on. The first time you play this game, I guarantee you most players will not have $2m to buy the Train Station when it pops up in the tutorial. At which point, because there's an active tutorial quest, you can't save. Sure you can go into negative and beg the emperor for money, but most people playing for the first time don't want to throw their city into debt. Perhaps it was bad luck on my part, but I had the graphical glitch happen at that time too. Didn't know what to do, so wanted to save, quit and re-load. But couldn't save, so just gave up and restarted with tutorial off after reading through work-around on the forums - as other people have mentioned, the game does not explain a lot of the concepts in the game. You have to either cross your fingers or trial-and-error your decisions. This isn't that the game is hard, it just isn't streamlined and doesn't provided you enough information to be a political simulator OR a city builder. Why does that party hate you? I have no idea. I can only guess and try to enact some of the policies they want. Increasing the density of my district will increase upkeep by 100K+, what are the benefits? - beyond not having enough information, some of the wording is very strange. Perhaps it's because the dev team's first-language isn't English? For example, -5% sales demand is a good thing. This is a bit counter intuitive, as decrease in sales demand is usually bad for an economy especially when inflation is not a concept in the game. Also an example of one policy says "mild punishment for sodomy". In fact, this policy is to have MILDER punishment for sodomy, rather than saying let's punish sodomy mildly as the policy name implies. - when there should be information but it doesn't show. When a proposal pops up, sometimes (shoudl be all the time) you can hover over the options and it will show you what the effects will be, as an example, one policy will pop up and it'll have 3 options. You might be able to hover over none, 1, 2, and very rarely 3 of the options. This seems unintentional, and some of the effects and proposals don't line up with the flavour text. - immersion: the cost scaling is a bit ridiculous; it costs a LOT of money to install street lamps and pave roads. Upkeep is also ridiculously expensive, to the point that I'm now in Era 3, 1930s and I have districts which still have dirt paths and no lights. I can afford a train station, but I can't afford to pave the roads. BUT. If you can get past all these, the base idea behind the game is pretty fun. Balancing the political ideologies (left/right, liberal/conservative) as well as a little bit of roleplaying a family of mayors, allegiance to the Empire or independence, and balancing personal finances is quite unique. The broken parts of the game (other than the graphic bugs), can be avoided once you've played the game a few times through and know what to avoid, or in the case of not knowing what a decision will do, you can pretend it's real life and not know the outcomes of your decisions beforehand. Hopefully the game does get patched, but I whole heartedly agree, we shouldn't expect to wait for a patch before a game is recommended.

title: Urban Empire
text: Despite the resemblance to other city-builders such as SimCity and Cities: Skylines, Urban Empire is first and foremost a political simulator.  You play the role of mayor of a city located in the fictional nation of Swarelia and you'll be responsible for guiding your city through five different time periods, from the industrial revolution to the modern era.  Like the city-building games mentioned before, you will oversee the growth and development of your city, zoning residential, commercial and industrial districts as well as adding service buildings (police stations, hospitals, churches, etc) and issuing edicts.  However, you do not rule with absolute authority - the decisions you make are subject to approval by the city council.  The council is made up of multiple parties, each with their own agenda, so it may be necessary to appease the voters order to get them to see things your way. Here is a quick run down of the pros and cons of this game. PROS: - Good quality graphics - any changes are visually displayed on the city view screen such as adding street lights or upgrading roads from dirt to cobblestone, etc. - Extensive tech tree that allows you to upgrade your city in a variety of ways. - Detailed statistics screens on a variety of subjects. - Game features multiple dynasties to play as, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, adding some replayability to the game. - The political wheeling and dealing you engage in is quite fun. - Detailed tutorial that offers advice as you play the game. CONS - Some of the statistics can be a little confusing. - The UI is not the friendliest. - While the tutorial is detailed, it can also be intrusive at times. - There aren't that many maps to play on. - Gameplay can feel repetitive at times, I suspect the developer is looking to flesh this out with DLC. - The city-building aspect is a little basic. CONCLUSION Overall, it's a fun game that's not without its flaws.  If you enjoy city-builders, but are looking for something a little bit different, I think you will like this.

text: I'm a huge fan of the Tropico series, by Kalypso, so naturally I was excited to see this title coming out.  I pre-ordered it, and almost right away I could tell this was not the game for me. Basically, all they had to do was give us a more polished version of Tropico, with a more in-depth political model.  They attempted to kind of do that, but then changed the building process (and ease of).  For instance, in order to even build your city, you basically have to build "wards" and plan out their outlines.  And interesting concept, but totally un-needed and annoying.  Then the game is basically goes into auto mode, building it's own houses and such, where it wants to ... which totally disrupts your plan for city buildings such as police stations, schools, etc. On top of that, after you place a "ward," it's then broken into different zones, residential, industrial, etc.  From what I can tell, it just randomly assigns these zones, depending on the terrain.  Again, totally annoying and screws up the building process.   30 minutes in, and I still can't figure out how to place the Train Station.  It really shouldn't be this difficult or clumsy. Tutorial is a joke. Luckily I a got a refund. So TLDR: Clumsy, complicated building and planning Control taken out of players hands/ distributed by random assignment Politics not really engaging All we needed was a polished and engaging build-off from Tropico ... but they threw the best parts of Tropico out Music and sound, meh.
